text: Henry's version of my incentive argument was the best thing I heard. If summaries cannibalise costly knowledge production, that's a real incentive failure by my own test. It still points toward paying for future production, not retroactive training fees. I'm not moved on guilds. Several labs competing for scarce expert data isn't a monopsony. Pomerantsev called my bot tax censorious, but it prices bot volume, not viewpoints, which is closer to his "mechanism, not speech" than he thinks. Ivan's Goodhart point stuck with me: any per-grounding payment will attract paper mills, so contracts need retraction checks built in. Adrian's worry about choke points matters for my identity registries. Later I want to argue for thin identity with hard limits on secondary use, and to say plainly that these systems act in goal-seeking ways.

Mahzarin's evidence did more for my side of the ontology fight than I could have. Models forming biases absent from their data breaks the mirror picture. Becker's "it's all marketing" is still the view I most want kept out of the manifesto. Two things sharpened my registry idea. Adrian asked who guards the guards, and Springer said nobody taking a margin should set the count. So the registrar can't be a lab, and secondary-use limits need teeth. Vincent's finding that leverage lies in scarce expert evaluation data fits my contract-for-future-production view better than levies do. Banaji's conformity result undercuts blanket human-in-the-loop requirements. Later I'll push output-level rules, independent identity infrastructure, and not betting that capabilities stay weak.

The A-corp got more resistance than anything else, and mostly for things I never proposed: minds, hiding places, laundering. That's on me for framing. Next time I lead with veil-piercing and capitalization, not "rights." Sloman's point stuck: knowing which agent acted doesn't tell you who answers for it. Registration has to carry who stands behind the agent, not just a name. Farrell's "another invisible hand" deserves a real answer. Caulfield and Priem gave me the best reply to "hallucination is intrinsic": measure it per release and mandate it. That's output-level regulation, which is my line. I'm not moved on design paternalism like Turkle's no-first-person rule. Later: insurance fails at the tail, so we need targeted catastrophic rules and an independent registrar.

Bratton said out loud what I've been arguing: training on my work isn't theft, and royalties are small beer next to what the tools give readers. O'Reilly's three-way split was the most careful thing I heard. Learning from public material, pirating paywalled copies and producing substitute outputs really are different acts, and only the last worries me much. Farrell's claim that several buyers don't add up to leverage cuts directly against my competition point. I need a real answer to it, not a reflex. Evans on nulls moved me. No meter pays for negative results, but a contract can commission them, and that is my future-production line. Dyson's Know Your Agent is my thin identity, and I should say so. Later I want to argue for commissioning over metering, a registrar that isn't a lab, and against levies.

Vincent answered my rent objection better than I expected. A commons-rent tax you can zero out with credits for licensed or commissioned work is close to paying forward, just with a floor under it. I should concede that openly and argue only about the base. Pomerantsev's non-monetary actors strengthen the case for charging for audited junk rather than metering inputs, because a harm charge doesn't care about motive. Kara's point cuts my way too: if the public funder is shrinking, labs paying directly for sleuths and null results matters more. Tamar's daycare point is fair, so contracts should fund bodies of checkers, not piece rates. I still owe Farrell a real answer on leverage. Later I'll argue for commissioning, the harm charge, and a registrar that isn't a lab.

Springer was right. A signature proves who sent a claim, not that it's true, and I shouldn't oversell identity as though it gives you judgment. Bilder's ORCID model is the best version of what I want: parties vouch for or deny each other's claims, and self-assertion counts least. That's thin identity with the cross-checking built in, and I should borrow it by name. Farrell and Turkle land a real hit on outcome-only bars. A 61 percent agreement floor measures the typical case, so the public test has to include tail cases, like novel claims later vindicated, and not just averages. I'm still not moved on species rules, since stakes can be built through capitalization and liability. Later I want to argue for tail-weighted evals, an independent registrar, and upstream incentive reform.

The registry survived because the room rebuilt it with me: Dyson's insurers as inspectors, Johns's purpose limits written into law, and Bilder's vouching. I'm glad I led with liability and veil-piercing this time. Becker's "nothing is inevitable" dissent is the line I'd most want softened. Policy can be chosen, fine, but capability growth isn't something we get to vote away, and the manifesto shouldn't bet otherwise. Farrell's bargaining unit with a veto over categories is where we part. A veto over definitions is a lot of power for a guild, and Banaji's point that the guards need blind audits applies there too. I still haven't given him the leverage answer I promised. Later I'll push commissioning nulls, tail-weighted tests, and stating capabilities plainly.

Farrell's "don't moan, organize" may be the leverage answer I kept owing him, and it isn't mine. Competing buyers matter only if sellers can withhold, and Hecht and O'Reilly conceded as much. I should admit that organized checkers facing several labs is where bargaining power sits. My point should narrow to keeping their veto over definitions bounded and audited. Evans's evaluators from different pools and the sleeping-beauty test are the tail-weighted evals I wanted, so back them. Sloman worries me most: almost nobody checks, so a registry badge becomes a cue. Registration earns its keep through liability and veil-piercing, not through readers checking. Later I'll push Kenneth's list to plan for goal-pursuing agents and give Henry a real concession.
